rv.q: This is breathtaking theatre with its own arresting imagination.
Full of enough thrills, scares and knowing nods to please fans and the uninitiated in equal measure
Standing ovations are ten a penny these days but this show thoroughly deserves the one it gets.
For all its mega-dollar hubris, Stranger Things: The First Shadow has a visceral impact.
The opening moments – involving the disappearance of a ship so huge it’s as if the Cutty Sark has broken into the stalls – are alone worth the ticket price.
This astounding show definitely feels like a new chapter in theatre.

Based on the phenomenally popular Netflix series, this visually stunning retro-horror romp is audacious, exhilarating and relentlessly inventive...Subtlety is not the goal here, and this show never quite matches the series’ charming mix of nostalgia, hope and horror. But it is an extraordinary, gripping spectacle.

Whether you are a die-hard fan poring over how this fits into the Stranger Things canon, or a Hawkins newbie feeling a little confused, The First Shadow is so mesmerising it is impossible not to be stunned by the spectacle of this electrifying show.

This isn’t a quiet, quaint, self-consciously theatrical little play. It’s a massive all-out event calculated to thrill fans of the award-winning Netflix series with explosions, thrills, and jumpscares galore
To be clear, if you're any sort of 'Stranger Things' fan and you can afford the ticket, it would be ridiculous for you not to go.

Everything shades, nothing detracts from the central performances, with Jatinder Singh Randhawa’s rumbling Porter, doubling as Seytan (with good play on the punning pronunciation), adding a note from the depths.
‘The First Shadow’ suffers from dramatic bloat and tonal inconsistency.
That Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson's play about the landmark climate change agreement is never remotely dull is a triumph against the odds to match the Protocol itself.
One is left simultaneously impressed and a little bewildered.
An intoxicating marriage of epic story and mesmerising theatricality makes this a must-see for fans

They're in search of a more visceral, live hit of the show's successful comedy-horror-sci-fi combination, and that's what director Stephen Daldry's eye-widening, often heart-racing production delivers.

There is a lot packed into the three hours that Stranger Things: The First Shadow plays (including interval), and sometimes it seems there is an information overload, but every moment grabs your attention as you try to sort out what is going on.
This is formidable, engaging theatre that is in productive dialogue with the resources of the screen, both narrative and formal.
Trapped in an ever more fastidious drive to stick to its canon and formula, the show struggles to step away from the TV blueprint or find new things to stay.
Everything here is ready to swallow you up faster than a demogorgon.
It’s not bad, but I drifted off on occasion, and still managed to easily follow proceedings, which to me is indicative of how it could be streamlined and speeded up.
Theatre at its very best, this play may have just turned the entire West End upside down.
The result is a success in its own right.
Stranger Things: The First Shadow was an extraordinary experience.
If you love the TV show, you will almost certainly love this.
This shiny three-hour-long transplant looks every penny of its eye-watering cost.
Suffice to say that while fans will love being immersed in a familiar world, The First Shadow stands alone as a remarkable piece of theatre.
This is Theatre of Sensation, Grand Guignol for the modern age.
Without a doubt, this is one of the most major and quality productions of the year.
Daldry and co-director Justin Martin have put on a gargantuan, fast-moving show that, for all the special effects, doesn't lose the humanity of the story.
These are only a few of the incredible people made this production possible; it has taken a massive team to make it genuinely magical, mind-blowing, and thrilling.

cn.t: Critics largely praise this visually spectacular prequel for its groundbreaking special effects and theatrical ambition, though some find the story unwieldy. Daldry's direction delivers thrilling stagecraft that wows fans and newcomers alike.
